stem: According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force on a small sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is
explanation: Stokes' law states F = 6πηrv: the drag is proportional to the radius and to the speed, each to the first power. A dependence on r² or v² is wrong for slow (streamline) motion; checking dimensions, ηrv = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹][L][LT⁻¹] = [MLT⁻²], a force, while ηr²v is not.

stem: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity is
explanation: From F = 6πηrv, η = F/(rv) has units N/(m × m s⁻¹) = N s m⁻², which is the pascal second (Pa s). The option N m⁻² s⁻¹ puts the second in the denominator, and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

stem: A sphere of radius 2 mm moves at 0.5 m s⁻¹ through water of viscosity 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s, slowly enough for Stokes' law to hold. The drag force on it is
explanation: F = 6πηrv = 6π × (1.0 × 10⁻³) × (2 × 10⁻³) × 0.5 = 6π × 10⁻⁶ N. The value 12π × 10⁻⁶ N uses the diameter 4 mm instead of the radius, and 6π × 10⁻³ N leaves the radius in millimetres.

stem: A small sphere moves through a viscous liquid. If its radius is halved and its speed is doubled, the Stokes' drag force on it becomes
explanation: F = 6πηrv is proportional to the product rv, and (r/2)(2v) = rv, so the drag is unchanged. Thinking that drag depends on the cross-sectional area (r²) would give half; in Stokes' law the radius appears only to the first power.

stem: A raindrop falling through air reaches its terminal velocity when
options: the air drag balances its weight
explanation: As the drop speeds up, the drag force grows until it equals the weight (upthrust in air is negligible); the net force is then zero and the drop falls with constant terminal velocity. The acceleration is g only at the start, when the drop is at rest and there is no drag.

stem: For a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid, the terminal velocity is vₜ = 2r²ρg/(9η), upthrust being neglected. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the terminal velocity becomes
explanation: vₜ ∝ r², so doubling r multiplies vₜ by 2² = 4. The weight grows as r³ (volume) while the drag at a given speed grows only as r, so their ratio gives r². Answering eight times uses the r³ of the weight and forgets the drag.

stem: A water droplet of radius 3 × 10⁻⁶ m falls through air of viscosity 2 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s. Using vₜ = 2r²ρg/(9η) with ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 10 m s⁻², and neglecting upthrust, its terminal velocity is
explanation: vₜ = 2 × (9 × 10⁻¹²) × 1000 × 10 / (9 × 2 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ / 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹. Using the diameter 6 × 10⁻⁶ m gives four times this, 4.0 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹, and dropping the factor 2/9 gives 4.5 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹.

stem: Two identical small raindrops, each falling with terminal velocity v, merge to form a single larger drop. Assuming Stokes' law, the terminal velocity of the larger drop is
explanation: The volume doubles, so the new radius is 2^(1/3) r. Since vₜ ∝ r², the new terminal velocity is (2^(1/3))² v = 2^(2/3) v = ∛4 v (about 1.6v). Answering 2v assumes the speed doubles with the mass, but the drag also grows with the larger radius.

stem: Which statement is true for streamline (laminar) flow of a fluid?
options: the velocity at a given point does not change with time
the fluid moves in irregular eddies
it occurs only at very high speeds
explanation: In streamline flow every particle passing a given point has the same velocity, so the velocity at each point stays constant in time and the layers slide smoothly past each other. Streamlines never cross, because a particle cannot have two velocities at one point. Eddies and high speeds are features of turbulent flow.

stem: Smoke rising from an incense stick moves smoothly at first and then breaks into swirls higher up. The swirling part is an example of
explanation: As the hot smoke speeds up, its smooth motion breaks into irregular, changing eddies: this is turbulent flow. The smooth lower column is laminar (streamline), which is the same as steady flow in which the velocity at each point does not change.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the assumptions made for an ideal fluid when deriving the equation of continuity and Bernoulli's equation?
explanation: An ideal fluid is taken as incompressible (constant density), non-viscous (no energy lost to friction) and in steady, streamline flow. Turbulent flow is the opposite of the steady flow assumed, so it is not an assumption. Incompressibility is the one most often forgotten; it is what lets the volume flow rate stay constant.

stem: The equation of continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, is a consequence of the conservation of
explanation: For an incompressible fluid in steady flow, the mass entering one end of a pipe each second must leave the other end: ρA₁v₁ = ρA₂v₂, giving A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Bernoulli's equation, not the continuity equation, comes from conservation of energy.

stem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional area falls to half its value at a narrow section. Compared with the wide section, the speed of the water in the narrow section is
explanation: From A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, halving the area doubles the speed. Four times would apply if the diameter (not the area) were halved, since the area then falls to a quarter.

stem: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ in a pipe of diameter 4 cm. The pipe narrows to a diameter of 2 cm. The speed of the water in the narrow part is
explanation: Area ∝ d², so halving the diameter makes the area one quarter and, by A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, the speed four times: v₂ = 2 × (4/2)² = 8 m s⁻¹. The value 4 m s⁻¹ treats the diameter ratio as the area ratio, forgetting to square it.

stem: Water comes out of a pipe of cross-sectional area 5 cm² at a speed of 2 m s⁻¹. The time taken to fill a 60 litre bucket is
explanation: Volume flow rate = Av = (5 × 10⁻⁴ m²)(2 m s⁻¹) = 1 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ = 1 L s⁻¹, so 60 L takes 60 s. The value 600 s comes from taking 5 cm² as 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²; since 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², the correct area is 5 × 10⁻⁴ m².

stem: While watering a lawn, Hamza partly covers the open end of a hose with his thumb, and the water shoots out much faster. This is explained by
explanation: The volume of water passing per second, Av, is fixed by the supply, so reducing the outlet area A increases the exit speed v, as the equation of continuity requires. Stokes' law concerns drag on a moving sphere, and Archimedes' and Pascal's principles concern fluids at rest.

stem: A hose of radius 1 cm carries water at 1 m s⁻¹ to a sprinkler head with 20 holes, each of radius 1 mm. The speed of the water leaving each hole is
explanation: Continuity: π(1 cm)² × 1 = 20 × π(0.1 cm)² × v, so 1 = 20 × 0.01 × v and v = 5 m s⁻¹. The value 100 m s⁻¹ forgets that the flow is shared among 20 holes, 0.5 m s⁻¹ uses the radius ratio 10 instead of its square, and 0.2 m s⁻¹ inverts the area ratio.

stem: Blood flows through the aorta, of cross-sectional area 3 cm², at 30 cm s⁻¹. If the total cross-sectional area of all the capillaries it feeds is 900 cm², the average speed of blood in the capillaries is
explanation: Continuity: 3 × 30 = 900 × v, so v = 90/900 = 0.1 cm s⁻¹. Although each capillary is very narrow, their combined area is huge, so the blood slows down; expecting it to speed up, as in a single narrow pipe, is the usual mistake.

stem: Bernoulli's equation for a fluid in steady flow is a statement of the conservation of
explanation: Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, comes from applying the work-energy principle to a moving fluid: the work done by pressure equals the change in kinetic and potential energy. Conservation of mass leads to the equation of continuity instead.

stem: Air flows steadily through a horizontal tube. According to Bernoulli's principle, where the speed of the air is greater, its pressure is
explanation: At the same height P + ½ρv² is constant, so a larger speed means a lower pressure. Many students expect faster air to push harder, but the extra kinetic energy is gained at the expense of pressure energy.

stem: In Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, each of the three terms represents
explanation: Each term has the units of pressure, N m⁻² = J m⁻³, so each is an energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy (½ρv²) and potential energy (ρgh) of one cubic metre of fluid. Energy per unit mass would be ½v² and gh, without the density ρ.

stem: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe. At one point its speed is 2 m s⁻¹ and its pressure is 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. At a narrower point the speed is 4 m s⁻¹. The pressure there is
explanation: For a horizontal pipe P₂ = P₁ − ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 2.0 × 10⁵ − 500 × (16 − 4) = 2.0 × 10⁵ − 6000 = 1.94 × 10⁵ Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 1.88 × 10⁵ Pa, and squaring the difference of the speeds, (4 − 2)², gives 1.98 × 10⁵ Pa.

stem: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose cross-sectional area changes from 0.02 m² to 0.01 m². The speed in the wider part is 3 m s⁻¹. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³, the pressure difference between the wide and narrow parts is
explanation: Continuity gives the narrow-part speed: v₂ = 3 × (0.02/0.01) = 6 m s⁻¹. Bernoulli then gives P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (36 − 9) = 1.35 × 10⁴ Pa. Dropping the ½ gives 2.7 × 10⁴ Pa, and using (6 − 3)² = 9 instead of 36 − 9 gives 4.5 × 10³ Pa.

stem: A water tank on a house roof in Peshawar has a small hole in its side 5 m below the water surface. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the speed with which water leaves the hole is
explanation: By Torricelli's theorem v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 5) = √100 = 10 m s⁻¹. The value 100 m s⁻¹ forgets the square root, and √50 m s⁻¹ leaves out the factor 2, which comes from ½v² = gh.

stem: Water flows out of a small hole near the bottom of a wide tank. If the depth of the hole below the water surface is made four times as great, the speed of efflux becomes
explanation: Torricelli's theorem gives v = √(2gh), so v ∝ √h and a fourfold depth doubles the speed: √4 = 2. Answering four times assumes v is proportional to h itself, which is true of the pressure at the hole, not of the speed.

stem: An open tank standing on the ground is filled with water to a height of 1.0 m. A small hole is made in its side 0.2 m below the water surface. The horizontal distance from the tank at which the jet strikes the ground is
explanation: Efflux speed v = √(2gh) with h = 0.2 m; the hole is 0.8 m above the ground, so the fall time is t = √(2 × 0.8/g). Range = vt = 2√(h × 0.8) = 2√0.16 = 0.8 m, independent of g. The value 0.4 m drops the factor 2 in the formula 2√(h(H − h)).

stem: In deriving Torricelli's theorem v = √(2gh) for water leaving a hole in a wide tank, it is assumed that
options: the pressure at the hole exceeds atmospheric
the flow through the hole is turbulent
the speed of the top surface is negligible
explanation: Applying Bernoulli's equation between the water surface and the hole, both are at atmospheric pressure, and because the tank is much wider than the hole the surface falls so slowly that its speed is taken as zero. This leaves ½v² = gh. The pressure at the free jet is atmospheric, not greater, and viscosity and turbulence are ignored, not assumed.

stem: A Venturi meter fitted in a water main is used to measure
options: the speed of flow in the pipe
explanation: A Venturi meter has a narrow throat; the pressure difference between the wide part and the throat, read from manometer tubes, gives the flow speed (and hence the flow rate) through Bernoulli's equation and continuity. It assumes a known density rather than measuring it, and viscosity is neglected.

stem: In a horizontal Venturi meter carrying water (density 1000 kg m⁻³), the area of the wide section is twice the area of the throat. The pressure in the wide section is 6000 Pa greater than in the throat. The speed of water in the wide section is
explanation: Continuity gives v₂ = 2v₁ in the throat. Bernoulli: 6000 = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (4v₁² − v₁²) = 1500v₁², so v₁² = 4 and v₁ = 2 m s⁻¹. The value 4 m s⁻¹ is the throat speed, and √12 m s⁻¹ comes from ignoring v₁ and writing 6000 = 500v².

stem: The two vertical manometer tubes of a Venturi meter show water levels that differ by 15 cm. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³, the pressure difference between the wide part and the throat is
explanation: ΔP = ρgΔh = 1000 × 10 × 0.15 = 1500 Pa. Using 15 cm as 1.5 m gives 1.5 × 10⁴ Pa, and dropping g gives 150 Pa; the height must be converted to metres first.

stem: The lift on the wing of an aeroplane in flight is mainly due to
options: higher pressure above the wing, where air moves faster
lower pressure below the wing, where air moves slower
equal pressure on both faces of the wing
lower pressure above the wing, where air moves faster
explanation: The wing's shape and tilt make air flow faster over the top surface than under it. By Bernoulli's principle, faster air has lower pressure, so the pressure below the wing is greater and the difference pushes the wing up. Slower air has higher, not lower, pressure.

stem: In the carburettor of a petrol engine, petrol is drawn into the air stream because
options: air slows in a narrow throat, raising its pressure
petrol becomes less viscous in the throat
air speeds up in a narrow throat, lowering its pressure
the throat heats the petrol until it boils
explanation: Air passing through the narrow throat (a Venturi) speeds up by continuity, so by Bernoulli's principle its pressure falls below that above the petrol, and petrol is pushed into the air stream through a jet. In a narrow section the air speeds up rather than slowing down, so its pressure falls rather than rises.

stem: During a strong windstorm, the light tin roof of a hut is lifted off. This happens because
options: pressure above the roof drops below that inside
pressure above the roof rises above that inside
pressure inside the hut drops sharply
the wind pushes directly upward on the roof
explanation: Fast wind over the roof has low pressure (Bernoulli), while the still air inside stays near atmospheric pressure. The higher pressure underneath pushes the roof upward. The wind blows horizontally, so it cannot push straight up, and the inside pressure does not suddenly fall.

stem: Two boats moving side by side, close together and parallel to each other, tend to be
explanation: Water squeezed into the narrow gap between the boats flows faster than the water on their outer sides, so the pressure between them is lower (Bernoulli). The higher outside pressure pushes the boats towards each other. Expecting faster water to push them apart is the usual error.

stem: In a perfume spray, squeezing the bulb sends a jet of air across the top of a narrow tube dipping into the perfume, and the perfume rises up the tube. This is mainly due to
options: capillary rise of the liquid in the narrow tube
high pressure produced by the fast air above the tube
viscous drag of the moving air pulling the liquid up
low pressure above the tube caused by the fast air
explanation: The fast air jet has low pressure (Bernoulli), so atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface in the bottle pushes the perfume up the tube, where the jet breaks it into a spray. Fast air lowers the pressure rather than raising it, and capillary rise is far too small to lift the liquid out of the tube.

stem: Honey flows much more easily on a hot day in Lahore than on a cold winter morning. This shows that, as the temperature of a liquid rises, its viscosity
explanation: Viscosity is internal friction between layers of the liquid; heating weakens the attraction between molecules, so the viscosity of a liquid decreases and it flows more easily. Increasing viscosity would make warm honey flow more slowly, which is the opposite of what is observed.

stem: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows up a pipe. At the lower end the speed is 2 m s⁻¹ and the pressure is 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The upper end is 2 m higher and has half the cross-sectional area. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the pressure at the upper end is
explanation: Continuity gives v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹. Bernoulli: P₂ = P₁ − ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) − ρgΔh = 1.5 × 10⁵ − 500 × 12 − 1000 × 10 × 2 = 1.5 × 10⁵ − 6000 − 20 000 = 1.24 × 10⁵ Pa. Leaving out the speed change gives 1.30 × 10⁵ Pa, and leaving out the height gives 1.44 × 10⁵ Pa.

stem: A steel ball of radius 3 mm and density 7800 kg m⁻³ falls through glycerine of density 1300 kg m⁻³ and viscosity 1.3 Pa s. Using vₜ = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), where σ is the density of the liquid, and g = 10 m s⁻², the terminal velocity is
explanation: vₜ = 2 × (3 × 10⁻³)² × (7800 − 1300) × 10 / (9 × 1.3) = 2 × 9 × 10⁻⁶ × 6500 × 10 / 11.7 = 1.17/11.7 = 0.10 m s⁻¹. Ignoring the upthrust (using 7800 instead of 6500) gives 0.12 m s⁻¹, and using the diameter 6 mm gives 0.40 m s⁻¹.

stem: Two steel balls of radii 1 mm and 3 mm fall through the same oil. Assuming Stokes' law holds, the ratio of their terminal velocities is
explanation: vₜ ∝ r² for the same materials, so the ratio is 1² : 3² = 1 : 9. The ratio 1 : 27 follows the weights (∝ r³) but forgets that the drag also grows with r, and 1 : 3 forgets the square.

stem: Smoke goes up a chimney more quickly when a wind blows across the top of the chimney, because
options: the wind raises the pressure at the chimney top
the wind cools and thickens the smoke
the wind lowers the pressure at the chimney top
the wind blocks outside air from entering
explanation: Moving air across the top of the chimney has lower pressure than the still air in the room below (Bernoulli), so the smoke is pushed up faster. A rise in pressure at the top would slow the smoke instead, and cooling would make the smoke denser and rise more slowly.

stem: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of
options: the mass of fluid per unit volume
how much its volume shrinks under pressure
the friction between its moving layers
explanation: Viscosity is the internal friction that resists one layer of fluid sliding over another; honey has a high viscosity and water a low one. Mass per unit volume is density and weight per unit volume is weight density, neither of which describes how easily the fluid flows.

stem: A ball of radius 1 cm moves slowly at 2 cm s⁻¹ through glycerine of viscosity 0.5 Pa s. Using Stokes' law, the drag force on the ball is
explanation: F = 6πηrv = 6π × 0.5 × 0.01 × 0.02 = 6π × 10⁻⁴ N, with r and v first converted to metres. Using the diameter 2 cm gives 1.2π × 10⁻³ N, and leaving the radius in centimetres gives 6π × 10⁻² N.

stem: Fatima drops a small steel ball from rest into a tall jar of oil. As the ball falls through the oil, its velocity
explanation: At first the ball accelerates, but the viscous drag grows with speed until drag plus upthrust equal the weight; then the net force is zero and the ball falls at constant terminal velocity. It cannot keep accelerating without limit because the drag keeps rising, and it starts from rest, so it is not constant from the start.

stem: A river of uniform depth becomes narrower as it passes between two rocks. In the narrow part the water flows
explanation: By the equation of continuity the volume of water passing each second, Av, stays the same, so where the cross-section A is smaller the speed v is greater. More slowly would mean less water passing per second through the gap, which would make water pile up upstream.

stem: Oil flows at 0.5 m s⁻¹ in a pipe of radius 3 cm, which then narrows to a radius of 1 cm. The speed of the oil in the narrow pipe is
explanation: Area ∝ r², so the area falls by a factor 3² = 9 and the speed rises by 9: v₂ = 0.5 × 9 = 4.5 m s⁻¹. The value 1.5 m s⁻¹ uses the radius ratio without squaring, and 13.5 m s⁻¹ cubes it.

stem: A large water tank in Quetta has a small tap 0.45 m below the water surface. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the speed of water flowing out of the open tap is
explanation: Torricelli's theorem: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.45) = √9 = 3 m s⁻¹. The value 9 m s⁻¹ forgets the square root, and √4.5 m s⁻¹ leaves out the factor 2.

stem: Air of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ flows over the top of a horizontal wing at 60 m s⁻¹ and under it at 50 m s⁻¹. The pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces is
explanation: ΔP = ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = 0.6 × (3600 − 2500) = 0.6 × 1100 = 660 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 1320 Pa, and squaring the difference of speeds, ½ρ(10)², gives only 60 Pa.

stem: A model aeroplane has a total wing area of 10 m². Air of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ moves over the upper surface at 70 m s⁻¹ and under the lower surface at 60 m s⁻¹. The lift force on the wings is
explanation: ΔP = ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = 0.6 × (4900 − 3600) = 780 Pa, and lift = ΔP × A = 780 × 10 = 7800 N. The value 780 N forgets to multiply by the area, 15 600 N forgets the ½, and 600 N uses (70 − 60)² instead of the difference of the squares.

stem: Bernoulli's equation in its simple form applies to
options: turbulent flow of a highly viscous fluid
any flow of a compressible gas at high speed
steady flow of an ideal fluid
a fluid at rest, never a moving one
explanation: Bernoulli's equation is derived for steady (streamline) flow of an ideal fluid, that is incompressible and non-viscous, so that no energy is lost to friction. Viscous, turbulent flow loses energy, and the equation also holds for a fluid at rest, where it reduces to P + ρgh = constant.

stem: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 2 litres per second through a horizontal pipe that narrows from a cross-sectional area of 4 cm² to 1 cm². The pressure difference between the wide and narrow parts is
explanation: Speeds: v₁ = (2 × 10⁻³)/(4 × 10⁻⁴) = 5 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = (2 × 10⁻³)/(1 × 10⁻⁴) = 20 m s⁻¹. Then ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (400 − 25) = 1.875 × 10⁵ Pa. Using (20 − 5)² gives 1.125 × 10⁵ Pa, and forgetting the ½ gives 3.75 × 10⁵ Pa.
